entries.title: Chaudhary helps Australia beat England in T20 shake-off of scandal-hit run
entries.summary: Australia beat England by three wickets with only one ball to spare as Nikhil Chaudhary's 66 leads charge in Melbourne.
entries.content:
Australia beat England by three wickets with only one ball to spare as Nikhil Chaudhary’s 66 leads the charge in Melbourne.

Nikhil Chaudhary blasted 66 and a late cameo from Jack Edwards helped Australia edge past England by three wickets with a ball to spare in the opening T20 International of the series.

Chaudhary’s 38-ball knock was crucial, but it was Edwards’ late flurry that got the job done, with the fast-bowler hitting an unbeaten 25 off 11 as they chased down a victory target of 188 on Saturday.

It ensured they took a 1-0 lead in the five-match series and temporarily lifted some of the clouds hanging over Australian cricket. Four of the country’s previous five matches have resulted in defeats, including a 2-1 One-Day International home series defeat by England.

The win also came on the day that Cricket Australia backed Pat Cummins to stay on as Test captain, despite continued allegations that he and the rest of the 2018 team were aware of the use of sandpaper to tamper with the ball during their tour of South Africa.

England captain Harry Brook’s quickfire 65 had guided the visitors to 187-9 – the highest T20I score at the Melbourne Cricket Ground – but Australia’s response had already begun prior to the chase when their bowlers restricted the end of the tourists’ innings that had looked set to comfortably pass 200.

“Right, there is the future of the Australian cricket side with those young guys in it,” said Australia captain Mitchell Marsh.

“They’re a great bunch. Hopefully a win like that gives them a lot of confidence that they all belong.”

The run chase started badly for Australia with opener Jake Fraser-McGurk falling to just his third ball, undone by the spin of Liam Dawson.

Australia got going when debutant Sam Harper came in and took 20 off Jamie Overton’s first over.

But the 29-year-old swung the bat once too often and departed for 32 off 15 balls, earning new England fast-bowler Henry Crocombe a first T20 wicket.

They were 86-2 at the halfway mark, and when Dawson took a stunning catch to remove Marsh for 37, Australia’s hopes appeared to rest with Tim David.

But the big-hitter struggled to get going and was out for 20, leaving Chaudhary, in only his fourth T20 for Australia, in charge.

He departed chasing another boundary, only for Edwards to step up.

They needed 11 of the last over from Sam Curran, and when Edwards smacked a six off the first delivery, they were on their way to the win.

“Very entertaining to go down to the last couple of balls,” said Brook. “We were probably 10 runs short of what we needed on that surface.”

Earlier, England lost opener Phil Salt to the first ball and they were 13-2 in the third over after Aneurin Donald was also removed cheaply for 10.

But Brook went to town, smacking three straight sixes from paceman Riley Meredith.

He reached 50 off 20 deliveries before his fiery knock ended when he got a faint outside edge off Chaudhary to wicketkeeper Harper.

Tom Banton was put down on 11, among six dropped catches by Australia, but his luck ran out on 39 when another debutant, Lachlan Shaw, held on to a difficult chance.

The wickets kept tumbling with Curran caught out on 21 and Will Jacks out lbw for three, with Jordan Cox hitting 27 to keep the scoreboard moving.

entries.title: Riemann hypothesis: Has the world’s most famous maths problem been cracked?
entries.summary: Mathematicians say the claimed proof, made with Claude, could be historic, but it may take weeks to understand it.
entries.content:
Mathematicians say the claimed proof, made with Claude, could be historic, but it may take weeks to understand it.

A mathematician from the tech giant Anthropic claims to have proven one of the world’s most famous – and most elusive – maths problems with the help of AI.

Levent Alpoge wrote on his website on Friday: “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.”

If his claim holds up, the proof he says he has would settle a question that has defeated mathematicians for 167 years. Independent experts are now trying to verify it, but so far no human has read through the entire argument.

Here is what we know.

What is the Riemann hypothesis?

First proposed by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in 1859, the hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers and is widely regarded as the most important open question in pure mathematics.

Prime numbers are whole numbers which can be divided only by one and themselves, such as 2, 3, 5 and 7. They appear to be scattered along the number line with no obvious pattern but the Riemann hypothesis proposes that their overall distribution actually follows a deep, hidden order – just one that humans have yet to identify.

“The Riemann hypothesis is the most famous and important unsolved problem in mathematics,” Abhishek Saha, professor of mathematics at Queen Mary University of London, told Al Jazeera.

“The patterns of the primes are encoded in a mathematical object called the Riemann zeta function, introduced by Bernhard Riemann in 1859.”

It is one of the seven Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problems, each carrying a $1m award.

What has the Anthropic mathematician claimed?

Alpoge, a member of the company’s technical staff, made the announcement on Friday in a four-page explanation posted on his website. He said the proof he has found covers the generalised Riemann hypothesis, which extends the original conjecture to a broader family of mathematical functions.

He did not publish a conventional paper. Alpoge released the argument in Lean, a programming language and proof assistant that checks reasoning step by step. He was open about how much of the work was Claude’s, writing that “Claude far outpaced me near the finish line”.

Kevin Buzzard, professor of pure mathematics at Imperial College London, said nobody yet understands what the proof actually shows.

“At the minute, we don’t even know why the theorem is true,” he told Al Jazeera. “It’s 17 million lines of Lean code, and this might correspond to tens of thousands of pages of mathematics. We don’t even yet know how much of this mathematics is new ideas, how much of it is just sort of standard stuff the machine just had to develop.

“At the minute, the proof is just millions of lines of gobbledygook written in a strange programming language,” he said. “And right now, as we speak, there’s people all over the world who are translating parts of this programming language back into English.”

He expects answers to come fairly soon, however. “Experience shows you that you give the humans the Lean code, and within a week or two, they have a much better understanding of what’s actually going on in this code,” he said.

Why is the Riemann hypothesis so important?

“The implications of this hypothesis extend across large parts of mathematics, and hundreds of other mathematical results have been proved assuming this hypothesis is true,” Saha said. “A proof would settle a question that has occupied some of the greatest mathematical minds for over 160 years.”

Buzzard said the result also matters beyond pure mathematics, including for internet security.

“We know there are some algorithms that we run where they’re very quick, but we don’t actually know for sure if they work,” he said. “They seem to work, and we know that if the generalised Riemann hypothesis is true, then they do work.”

He said cryptographers had long worked on the assumption that the Riemann hypothesis is true. “In practice, people do tend to assume that the Riemann hypothesis is true because it’s a viable hypothesis to assume, because there’s so much evidence that it’s true,” he said. “But we can sleep slightly safer in our beds at night because it is true.”

Buzzard said the result stands out among recent AI breakthroughs in mathematics. He compared it with the Navier-Stokes problem, another Millennium Prize problem, which OpenAI said an unreleased AI model had solved in September. “That one doesn’t really have any applications at all,” he said, calling it “just of theoretical interest”. “Whereas the Riemann hypothesis has applications to neighbouring fields.

“It’s a very hard problem, but it’s definitely not the hardest problem in mathematics,” he said, pointing to even stronger versions such as the “extended Riemann hypothesis and the grand Riemann hypothesis”.

“The Riemann hypothesis is just, in some sense, at the foot of a mountain,” he said. “We’re beginning our trek up the mountain with this theorem.”

Why has it remained so elusive for so long?

“The problem is relatively simple to state, but extraordinarily difficult to prove,” Saha said. “Mathematicians have developed vast amounts of sophisticated theory in their attempts to solve it, but none of the techniques developed over the past 167 years has been sufficient. The direct methods have all been tried, and none of them come close to resolving it.

“Until very recently, most mathematicians, myself included, believed that a proof would require substantial new mathematical theories, perhaps developed over the next few decades.”

He said the claimed proof had overturned his expectations. “My own intuition was that we were still several years away from a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. This claimed proof, if correct, shatters my model of reality,” he said.

“If difficult problems are like valuable mineral reserves buried miles underground, you first need to build the infrastructure to reach them. What this proof seems to have done is something completely different. It takes an incredibly complicated tour through the infrastructure built to reach a hundred other mineral reserves, situated far from the original destination, and somehow creates a wormhole to that destination.”

Buzzard said it is still too early to know what humans had been missing. “There is a chance that there were no ideas that the humans were missing. There is a chance that all of the ingredients were there, that nobody had just been smart enough to put everything together,” he said. “There is a chance that there’s a thousand pages of new ideas, very deep new theories.”

“Right now, we honestly can’t tell you, because nobody understands the proof of it. That will change. In a matter of weeks, that will change.”

What role is AI playing in solving major mathematical problems?

The past year has been one of AI-driven advances in mathematics. An earlier AI-assisted result showed that at least 67.25 percent of a particular set of mathematical values follow the pattern predicted by the Riemann hypothesis. The new claim, if correct, would extend this to all of them.

“AI is creating a revolution in mathematics,” Saha said. “It is helping us solve problems previously thought out of reach and, in doing so, it will undoubtedly lead to the creation of new mathematics. However, this also means that the way mathematicians have traditionally conducted research will no longer be how it is done in the future.

“Asking the right questions, creating new research directions, writing good expositions, and acting as an effective director or conductor for AI will become increasingly important, while technical brilliance in constructing proofs may become less so.”

He argued that the credit should go to Alpoge. “Much of the press is referring to this as a proof by Claude. I think they should instead credit the person involved: Levent Alpoge,” he said. “Others with similar access to frontier AI models and computing resources were not able to come up with a proof of the Riemann hypothesis.

“This proof shows that a brilliant mathematician can direct and orchestrate AI in ways that allow them to prove theorems others cannot. The honour of proving RH, if the proof holds up, belongs largely to him. He should get a Fields Medal for this.” The Fields Medal is a prestigious mathematics prize awarded every four years by the International Congress of Mathematicians (ICM) to mathematicians under age 40.

Do we even need humans to do maths any more?

Buzzard rejected fears that AI has made human mathematicians redundant. “The rumours that maths is dead have been greatly exaggerated,” he said. “What’s actually happening is that mathematics has a very exciting and powerful brand new tool.”

“Mathematics is infinitely big. You can’t solve all of it,” he said. He compared AI with the telescope. “Historically, astronomers were just staring at the sky, right? And then the telescope was invented, and all of a sudden we can see everything much, much more clearly.

“The AI doesn’t have taste, not yet anyway. You tell it what to do, and it does it,” he said. “We’ve basically got our own telescope.”

Buzzard said AI was “beginning to democratise” mathematics, although for now the breakthroughs are concentrated in a few firms. “Currently, it is the tech companies with access to the new internal models who are doing the best breakthroughs right now, but this will change as more powerful models become available to the public and the tech companies lose interest.”

He said some of the unease among mathematicians is about loss. “They are grieving because the field is changing rapidly, and with change comes loss. We will do mathematics in new ways going forward, and some people will miss the old ways,” he said.

“The other reason people are upset is that it has hurt a lot of people’s egos. Humans were the best at mathematics, and the best humans would prove theorems, and the theorems would be named after them.”

entries.title: Russia says Kaliningrad-bound ship struck by drones in Gulf of Finland
entries.summary: Two drones attack a cargo ship close to Russia's maritime border, causing damage and crew evacuation.
entries.content:
Two drones attack a cargo ship close to Russia’s maritime border, causing damage and crew evacuation.

Rescue efforts are under way in the Gulf of Finland after a Russian cargo ship was hit by drones close to Russia’s maritime border.

The ship, the Sparta II, is on fire and has now drifted into Finnish territorial waters, authorities say.

Finland’s Ministry of Defence said its forces had detected a drone attack on a Russian vessel in international waters, with the vessel sustaining damage, and dispatched Finnish Border Guard units to the scene.

A photograph taken by a Border Guard patrol plane shows flames and thick smoke coming from the rear of the ship.

The attack happened west of Gogland Island on Saturday morning, with Finland temporarily instating air and sea traffic restrictions in the eastern part of the gulf.

Finland’s Border Guard said the vessel is known to have links to the Russian armed forces.

According to the Border Guard, the crew of the Sparta II have not been forced to abandon ship, and there has been no environmental damage so far from the drone attack, while the vessel is in the open sea off the southern coastal town of Loviisa.

“The Border Guard is preparing to evacuate people and assist in firefighting operations,” Finnish authorities said.

It is not clear who was behind the attack, but Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo wrote on X that “war is spilling over into our immediate vicinity. The Finnish authorities are handling the situation in the Gulf of Finland, where a drone strike has hit a Russian merchant vessel. Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor.”

Alexander Drozdenko, governor of Russia’s Leningrad region, said the damage had yet to be fully assessed.

“Three nautical miles from the Russian Federation’s border, a cargo vessel bound for Kaliningrad was attacked by two drones,” he wrote on the messaging app Max.

Kaliningrad’s Governor Alexey Besprozvannykh said supplies to the Russian exclave were not at risk.

The Gulf of Finland is a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea between Finland and Estonia, both NATO members. It connects Russia’s former capital of Saint Petersburg with its Kaliningrad enclave by sea.

Finland’s Ministry of Defence said air and sea traffic restrictions had been put in place as a precaution in case further drones needed to be intercepted, adding that Finland had notified its allies of the incident.

Ukraine and Russia have attacked each other’s shipping throughout the war, mostly in the Black Sea.

Earlier this month, Finland’s military said it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland, which Ukraine took credit for. Helsinki said it had raised concerns with Kyiv about striking in the area afterwards.

entries.title: Sudan’s elderly face hardship and heartbreak in a life of displacement
entries.summary: Sudan's displaced elderly often have to support grandchildren or fend for themselves.
entries.content:
Sudan’s displaced elderly often have to support grandchildren or fend for themselves.

Khartoum, Sudan – Hamad Mohammed Adam, 70, should be spending his days surrounded by his family and enjoying the comfort of life in his home village. Instead, he finds himself among hundreds of displaced elderly people in a camp in western Omdurman, with little between him and death.

Three months ago, Adam’s life changed when the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary attacked his village near Bara, northern Kordofan. He followed the rest of the village and fled, leaving behind his home, belongings and most painfully, his family.

“It was an early morning last August when the Rapid Support Forces militia invaded our village near Bara. It was a terrifying morning; they were killing everyone, women, men, children,” he said. “I ran with some friends and spent days to reach Omdurman. I am lucky that I have survived, but I am worried about my family.”

The war between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the RSF paramilitary, two former military allies now engaged in a bitter power struggle for Sudan since April 2023, has affected all parts of the country. When fighting erupts in one area, residents are often forced to flee to another, where they lack jobs, a home, or a support base.

After travelling for about 300km (186 miles), Adam found himself in western Omdurman, close to the capital Khartoum. Today, he resides at al-Moulih camp for displaced people in western Omdurman, home to approximately 10,000 people, with those aged over 65 accounting for about one in five residents.

His escape from the fighting between the SAF and RSF, which has triggered one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, was only the start of his troubles. Adam knows nothing about the whereabouts of his family, and they don’t know where he is.

Lacking the support of his family, Adam’s immediate concern is finding enough food, medication and healthcare to survive. But the uncertainty of his family’s fate weighs heavily on him every day.

In the same camp, Aisha Alneel, 70, has lost more than her home: The security, independence and family connections that once shaped her life. She’s accompanied by her 72-year-old sister who needs medical attention, and her greatest hope is to reunite with her family and regain some sense of normality.

“I came to Port Sudan two years ago after losing my home in Khartoum. My plan is to travel with my older sister, but we faced financial strain,” she said. “We preferred to stay at this displacement camp in Port Sudan until we have enough money to leave.”

Sudan’s older population, classified as aged above 65 by the United Nations, is 1.8 million people in 2026, accounting for 3.5% of the population, according to the UN’s Economic and Social Commission for Western Asia.

Many elderly displaced people depend on regular medical supervision and assistance with everyday activities. When conflict forces them to abandon their homes, families, and familiar environments, these essential support systems can disappear overnight. It also disrupts or destroys the infrastructure and services they relied on to maintain a dignified life.

Traditionally, Sudanese families and local communities played a central role in caring for older relatives. Younger family members often assisted with food, medical appointments and daily needs, but the war has seen families scattered across Sudan and the country’s social fabric destroyed.

Living standards have plunged to levels last seen in the early 1990s, making it difficult for families to survive, let alone provide support to others. The UNDP has noted that Sudan’s economy has shrunk by more than 40 percent since the war broke out, and extreme poverty is expected to rise above 60 percent. This has placed additional pressure on institutions responsible for caring for older people.

At Al-Daw Hajooj home for the elderly, the management faces the difficult task of providing care to senior citizens amid a wider humanitarian crisis.

Moubarak Satti, director of Al-Daw Hajooj, told Al Jazeera that the home has 11 seniors and the situation remains “difficult” due to a lack of financial support needed to run the elderly care programmes.

“Like many institutions, we have been severely affected by the war. We lost our only vehicle, which we use it to transport elderly people to medical facilities; we lost many people during the conflict due to the lack of medical care,” Satti said.

“We welcome financial support from the community, NGOs, and international humanitarian organisations to continue providing care and essential services to older people.”

This requires more than emergency food assistance. It needs a coordinated response that recognises elderly people as a particular group with specific needs, said Satti.

The strain of displacement also impacts older people’s mental and emotional wellbeing. Separation from children and grandchildren, uncertainty about the future, and feelings of anxiety and helplessness can create intense feelings of isolation, government officials have said.

The Khartoum State Ministry of Social Development has provided support to vulnerable groups, such as the elderly, coordinating social protection services and working with relevant institutions to respond to the needs of displaced communities.

But the scale of the problem is staggering, with about 8.6 million people currently displaced. Attacks on civilian areas have also severely disrupted public services, making government and NGO support increasingly challenging, Minister of Social Welfare Siddig Ferini told Al Jazeera.

“We have reunited dozens of elderly displaced people with their families in many Sudanese states, while others are still searching for loved ones,” Ferini said. “We call on humanitarian organisations, donors, and philanthropists to support elderly people through social care and essential services, especially amid the ongoing war and economic crisis.”

entries.title: Israeli attacks on Gaza kill at least four Palestinians
entries.summary: Israeli drone attack kills three people in Gaza City; another is shot dead by Israeli forces in Jabalia.
entries.content:
Three Palestinians were killed in an Israeli drone attack while a Palestinian man was killed by gunfire in Jabalia.

Israeli attacks in Gaza have killed at least four Palestinians in violation of last year’s “ceasefire”, as winter flooding deepens the humanitarian crisis in the enclave.

At least three people were killed when a van delivering food to displaced people was struck by an Israeli drone on Saturday in the Tal al-Hawa neighbourhood of Gaza City.

Separately, a Palestinian man was killed by Israeli gunfire in the Halawa displacement camp, east of northern Gaza’s Jabalia refugee camp.

Al Jazeera’s Ibrahim al-Khalili, reporting from Gaza City, said the van was “a humanitarian vehicle meant to deliver aid and assistance”. The man shot in Halawa was taken to al-Shifa Hospital, he said.

Earlier on Saturday, an Israeli attack targeted a young man on an electric bicycle in al-Mawasi, in Khan Younis in southern Gaza, al-Khalili said. Three people were injured and taken to Nasser Medical Complex.

“The ceasefire has yet to deliver a change for the people in Gaza,” he said. “Israeli attacks and gunfire have been part of the grim reality for the people in Gaza.”

Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has continued despite a so-called “ceasefire”, which came into force last October. More than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since then.

Settler violence in the West Bank

The ongoing attacks on the enclave coincide with a surge in pogroms carried out by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank.

Late on Friday, Hamza Masoud Salim Abdo, 42, was shot dead by security guards from an illegal Israeli settlement near the village of Dura al-Qar, north of Ramallah.

The Palestinian Health Ministry said his body was being withheld by Israeli authorities. Another Palestinian man was detained during the incident.

Reporting from Ramallah in the West Bank, Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh said settlers have been carrying out attacks with “impunity”.

“Less than 3 percent of Israeli attacks that are investigated lead to a partial or full conviction by Israeli authorities. Also, the number of settler attacks reported to Israeli authorities is very, very low because Palestinians are often detained, questioned or harassed for filing reports against violent settlers,” Odeh reported.

The violence inflicted on Palestinians in the West Bank has been condemned by Israeli allies, including the United Kingdom. Critics say Western leaders have not supported their rhetoric with sufficient action.

Earlier this month, an Al Jazeera investigation found that the UK had awarded $14.4m in new public contracts to firms with links to illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank, despite recently announcing a ban on importing goods from such settlements.

The British government has also sanctioned companies involved in settlement expansion.

‘Uncertain’ days ahead

Winter weather has compounded the humanitarian crisis in Gaza, with the World Food Programme (WFP) warning earlier this week that Palestinians have been forced to burn rubbish to cook their food.

“Now even the rubbish is wet,” warned Shaun Hughes, WFP’s country director for Palestine.

The International Organization for Migration (IOM) has said that more than 100,000 tents in Egypt cannot be delivered to Gaza due to strict conditions imposed by Israel.

“Usually anything under 38 millimetres is okay; anything above, it’s usually deemed as not acceptable,” Hughes explained.

“It is not a statement of dual use; it is just that this tent at this time is not allowed to enter Gaza … We don’t get the specifics,” said Karl Baker, head of the IOM’s Gaza programme.

Al Jazeera’s al-Khalili, reporting from Gaza, said: “The coming days are uncertain and the lack of basic necessities looms.”

Gaza’s Health Ministry reported on Saturday that 1,671 people had been killed since the “ceasefire” came into effect in October 2025. Al-Khalili said Israel has committed more than 600 ceasefire violations since then.

Meanwhile, 74,736 Palestinians have been killed since Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza three years ago.

entries.title: Pakistan drop Rizwan and Masood, but back Babar and Agha in overhaul
entries.summary: Former captains Mohammad Rizwan and Shan Masood lose Pakistan central contracts, but Babar Azam and Salman Agha backed.
entries.content:
Former captains Mohammad Rizwan and Shan Masood lose Pakistan central contracts, but Babar Azam and Salman Agha backed.

Pakistan’s Cricket Board has announced that it will drop former captains Mohammad Rizwan and Shan Masood in a major overhaul of its central contract list.

Saturday’s announcement, which expands the pool of contracted players to 38 ⁠from 30, comes a day after Pakistan won the second Test against Sri Lanka in Rawalpindi, marking a first series win in two years.

“We are testing new players and these contracts are devised to let players focus on their specific format,” Pakistan selector Aaqib Javed told the media.

The board overhauled the Test squad after the second Test in its disastrous 3-0 defeat against England, sending seven players home and sacking head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed.

White-ball head coach Mike Hesson was given the Test team in a bid to lift the country, which is currently ninth and last in the 2025-27 World Test Championship cycle.

Besides Rizwan and Masood, white-ball specialist Saim Ayub, spinner Noman Ali and pace bowler Hasan Ali are among the 12 players who have been removed from contracts.

Test skipper Babar Azam and recently sacked Twenty20 International (T20I) skipper Salman Agha are in the top category of the 38-player list.

“The ‘AB’ category is for Test and ODIs, ‘A’ for Test-only, ‘BC’ for ODI and T20I players; ‘C’ for T20I specialists; ‘D’ for development players,” said Javed.

The new contracts run from July 2026 to June 2027. Players had been without central contracts since the ⁠expiry of the previous cycle in June.

The PCB had said at that time that only male cricketers who had played at least four tests, six one-day internationals ‌or six Twenty20s in the previous 12 months would be eligible for central contracts.

Under the new system, contracts are split into five specialised categories: tests and ODIs, Test specialists, ODIs and T20Is, T20I ⁠specialists, and emerging players in ⁠the developmental pathway.

The new contracts run through June 30, 2027. Players had been without central contracts since the ⁠expiry of the previous cycle in June.
